title: Whirling southern star trails over ALMA
caption: Southern star trails over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Great whorls of stars swirl above ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, in this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi. The pattern recalls van Gogh's Starry Night, or perhaps the view from a spaceship leaping into hyperspace.

In fact, the circles trace Earth's rotation, revealed by a long exposure. In the southern hemisphere, the stars seem to wheel around the south celestial pole, found in the faint constellation of Octans, the Octant, between the better-known Southern Cross and the Magellanic Clouds. Given a long enough exposure, each star draws its own circular trail. Some antennas look blurred because they were moving while observing during the shot.

The photo was taken on the Chajnantor plateau, 5000 meters up in the Chilean Andes, home of ALMA. ALMA studies the cool Universe, including molecular gas and dust and the relic radiation from the Big Bang. When the photograph was released, ALMA was still under construction, but early science had already begun.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure landscape photograph. The source gives no camera settings beyond the long exposure.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and only a long camera exposure turns Earth's rotation into these circular trails.

explore: ALMA was planned to have 54 antennas 12 meters across plus twelve 7-meter antennas. Europe, North America and East Asia run it jointly with Chile, and it is led for Europe by ESO, for North America by NRAO and for East Asia by NAOJ.
alt: Circular star trails swirling above ALMA antennas, some slightly blurred, on a high desert plateau.
